query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a protective oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C is controlled by the ability of the reactive element X, in synergy with chromium, to rapidly diffuse and segregate to the alloy surface. When X (especially Al) diffuses sufficiently to concentrate at the metal/oxide interface, it promotes the nucleation of a continuous, low‐diffusivity oxide (e.g., Al2O3 and/or Cr2O3) that grows slowly and accommodates thermal stresses. In contrast, when the diffusion kinetics or surface enrichment of X is less favorable (as with Si or Mn), the oxide scale forms more rapidly but is inhomogeneous and prone to cracking or spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys processed into a homogeneous single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state with uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloys to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere maintained above 900 °C under controlled conditions.
generation.conditions: Isothermal high-temperature oxidation tests performed above 900 °C with controlled heating rates and dwell times in air or a corrosive medium.
generation.structural_mediator: The selective diffusion and surface segregation of chromium and the reactive element X at phase boundaries and interfaces, which mediate the formation of a continuous, adherent, and low-diffusivity oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: A balanced flux exists between the outward diffusion of reactive metal atoms (primarily X and Cr) and the inward penetration of oxygen. In alloys where X (notably Al) diffuses rapidly and uniformly to the surface, a coherent protective oxide forms that grows slowly (following parabolic kinetics) and relieves thermal expansion stresses. When X does not effectively segregate or when its diffusion is nonuniform, the resulting oxide scale is thick, noncoherent, and susceptible to cracking/spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with optimal reactive element enrichment (e.g., those with Al) will exhibit a thin, dense, and slow-growing oxide scale with parabolic oxidation kinetics and high adherence, whereas alloys with Si or Mn as X will develop faster-growing, inhomogeneous oxides that crack and spall under high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: Comparable CrFeCoNi alloys without the beneficial reactive element addition or with inadequate surface segregation of X will form non-protective, rapidly thickening oxide scales prone to cracking under identical high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in a homogeneous single- or multiphase solid-solution state exposed to isothermal high-temperature oxidation (>900 °C) under controlled atmospheric compositions; deviations in alloy homogeneity, microstructural phase segregation, or reactive element concentration may fall outside the effective regime.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative details of the diffusion rates and the critical enrichment threshold for X remain uncertain and may depend on subtle microstructural nuances; hence, the exact kinetics of oxide growth and the stress accommodation processes warrant further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples where X is systematically varied among Al, Si, and Mn, ensuring identical processing and microstructural homogeneity. Subject each alloy to isothermal oxidation at a temperature above 900 °C under a controlled oxidative or corrosive environment. Ensure that sample geometry, surface preparation, and exposure time are uniform across the series.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and growth kinetics (to determine parabolic vs. linear behavior) via thermogravimetric analysis and cross-sectional SEM
Surface and interfacial microstructure and chemical composition via electron microscopy (EDS) and XRD to assess continuity and phase identity of the oxide
Mechanical testing (e.g., adhesion, indentation) to examine the integrity of the oxide layer and the presence of cracks or spallation
Diffusion profiles of reactive elements (X and Cr) from the bulk to the surface using depth-profiling techniques (e.g., SIMS or STEM-EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with the reactive element X expected to promote protective oxide formation (e.g., with Al) do not demonstrate a significantly thinner, more coherent, and slowly growing oxide layer compared to alloys with Si or Mn under identical test conditions, or if no correlation is found between the measured diffusion/segregation of X and the improved oxide stability, then the hypothesis is refuted.

Various stability criteria developed for high-entropy alloys are applied to compositions produced by mechanical alloying. While they agree with the annealed samples, these criteria fail to describe the as-milled metastable systems, highlighting the ability of mechanical alloying to overcome the limitations imposed by these criteria. The criteria are based on atomic size (Ω ≥ 1.1 and δr ≤ 6.6%) and/or electronegativity misfit, as well as on mixing enthalpy (Λ>0.95 J mol−1K−1 and −5 kJ mol−1<∆Hmix<0), or purely thermodynamic (ϕYe>20; ϕKing>1; Teff<500 K). These criteria are applied to several compositions found in the literature and to two metastable fcc solid solutions produced by mechanical alloying with compositions Al0.75CoXFeNi with X = Cr and Mn. Single-phase microstructures are stable up to above 600 K, leading to more stable multiphase systems after annealing above this temperature. Mössbauer spectrometry shows that, whereas the alloy with Cr is paramagnetic in the as-milled and annealed state, the alloy with Mn changes from paramagnetic to ferromagnetic behavior (Curie temperature ~700 K) after annealing. The concept of mixing equal or near equal amounts of elements to fabricate new alloys has sparked worldwide interest in alloy design. The approach is based on mixing multiple principal elements (MPE) in relatively high (often equiatomic) concentrations and stands in sharp contrast to the traditional practice of adding minor alloying elements. Though much emphasis is given to enhancing the mechanical properties while designing MPE alloys (MPEAs), understanding the corrosion and oxidation behavior of these alloys is an emerging research area. The MPEAs based on transition elements, such as CoCrFeNiMnAl (referred to as high entropy alloys or HEAs), have shown improved combinations of strength, ductility, and strain hardenability,. The structure and stability of HEAs surface oxides, however, are not well understood largely due to a wide variety of compositions and limited understanding of the underlying atomic-scale mechanisms of the oxidation process. The simulation results match the experimental findings reported in the literature to a reasonable extent, suggesting that we have indeed captured a significant amount of the underlying physics of the process. drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloys (with X = Si, Mn, or Al), the ability to form a stable, coherent, and slow‐growing protective oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by the preferential oxidation of the reactive element X (and Cr) that produces a continuous, low‐diffusivity oxide phase (e.g., silica or alumina) at the metal–oxide interface. This scale accommodates thermal expansion and minimizes stress buildup, thereby resisting cracking or spallation. An optimal concentration of X is required to promote the consistent formation of this protective phase, while alloys with lower or non‐optimal enrichment will tend to develop thicker, inhomogeneous, and unstable oxides that crack under thermal strain.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high‐entropy alloys in a single‐ or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, where X is Si, Mn, or Al.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloy samples to a high-temperature (>900 °C) oxidative or corrosive atmosphere.
drafts.conditions: Controlled high-temperature conditions (above 900 °C) in a defined oxidative or corrosive environment with set oxygen partial pressures over prolonged exposure times to simulate service conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent, and compositionally enriched oxide layer at the substrate interface that mediates the accommodation of thermal stresses and restricts oxygen transport.
drafts.mechanism: The reactive element X (along with Cr) oxidizes preferentially to form a protective oxide phase (e.g., silica from Si or alumina from Al) which has inherently slow growth kinetics and low oxygen diffusivity. This oxide layer develops a coherent interface with the underlying metal, mitigating stress buildup and preventing scale spallation during thermal cycling. Insufficient enrichment or improper phase distribution (especially in multiphase microstructures) leads to inhomogeneous oxide growth, resulting in cracking and spallation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys with an adequate level of the reactive element will display a thin, uniform, and slowly thickening oxide layer that remains adherent even after prolonged exposure above 900 °C, while alloys with lower reactive element content or less favorable phase distributions will develop thicker, unstable oxide scales that crack and spall under the same conditions.
drafts.baseline: The baseline is defined by comparable CrFeCoNi alloys lacking the optimized concentration of the reactive element X—in which a coherent and well-adherent oxide layer does not form, resulting in rapid oxide growth with prevalent cracking and spallation.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies under service conditions of high-temperature oxidation (>900 °C) in defined oxidative or corrosive atmospheres and is most relevant for alloy compositions maintained in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX alloy samples with systematically varied concentrations of the reactive element X (Si, Mn, or Al) while keeping all other alloying elements constant. Expose these samples to a controlled high-temperature environment (>900 °C) under an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere for identical time periods. Use electron microscopy, spectroscopy, and diffraction techniques to analyze the nature, thickness, uniformity, and adherence of the oxide layers formed on each sample.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and growth rate over time
Chemical composition profiles across the metal–oxide interface
Microstructural characterization of oxide phases (e.g., presence of continuous silica or alumina layers)
Incidence and pattern of cracking/spallation of the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with the targeted optimal reactive element enrichment do not develop a coherent, slow-growing, and adherent oxide layer (or if such protective behavior is observed equally in samples with suboptimal reactive element levels), then the hypothesis that the optimized reactive element concentration solely governs the protective oxide formation by promoting a stable interfacial phase is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (where X = Si, Mn, or Al), the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by the synergistic effect of Cr’s selective oxidation and the minor element’s role in modifying grain-boundary and scale–substrate interfacial chemistry. This combination promotes the formation of a continuous Cr-rich oxide scale that adjusts interfacial stresses and minimizes cracking/spallation.
drafts.material_initial_state: A homogenized single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state of CrFeCoNiX with controlled microstructure and uniformly distributed minor element X.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloy to a high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidative or corrosive atmosphere.
drafts.conditions: Temperature maintained above 900 °C in a controlled oxidative or corrosive environment, ensuring steady thermal conditions and atmosphere composition for prolonged exposures.
drafts.structural_mediator: A coherent, continuous Cr-rich oxide scale with dopant-induced modifications (segregation or enrichment of X at critical interfaces such as grain boundaries and the oxide/metal interface) that improve stress relaxation and adhesion.
drafts.mechanism: Cr selectively oxidizes to form a protective scale; concurrently, the minor element X alters local chemistry (e.g., at grain boundaries) to reduce defect densities and lower differential thermal expansion stresses. This mitigates the accumulation of stresses that would otherwise lead to oxide cracking or spallation, resulting in a slow-growing but persistent protective layer.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under the defined high-temperature oxidative/corrosive conditions, the CrFeCoNiX alloy will form a slow-growing, adherent, and mechanically robust oxide layer that remains mostly intact (with minimal cracking or spallation) over prolonged exposure, in contrast to similar alloys lacking the beneficial influence of X.
drafts.baseline: Comparable alloys (e.g., CrFeCoNi without the advantageous role of X, or CrFeCoNiX alloys with suboptimal distribution of X) which typically develop more defect-prone, non-coherent, and rapidly spalling oxide layers.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for alloys with uniform single- or multiphase solid-solution microstructures and within a specific compositional window for X; deviations in alloy homogeneity, phase segregation, or excessive X content might fall outside the effective regime.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one group of CrFeCoNiX alloys with a controlled and uniform distribution of X and a baseline set lacking the beneficial configuration of X (or completely without X). Expose both sets to a controlled oxidative environment at temperatures >900 °C for extended periods. Use in situ thermal microscopy to monitor oxide growth and ex situ cross-sectional electron microscopy (with EDS and XRD analyses) to evaluate scale continuity, interface adhesion, and defect densities.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and growth rate over time
Crack density or evidence of spallation on the oxide surface
Chemical composition mapping across the oxide scale and at the oxide/metal interface
Microstructural characterization of any interfacial modifications correlated with the presence of X
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the CrFeCoNiX alloys and the baseline alloys exhibit similar oxide growth kinetics, mechanical integrity, and defect characteristics (such that the presence of X does not correlate with improved oxide stability or reduced cracking/spallation), the hypothesis would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, a stable and coherent protective oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C will form when the reactive element X (Al, Si, or Mn) diffuses rapidly enough to enrich the metal/oxide interface so that it nucleates a slow‐growing oxide (e.g., a continuous Al2O3, SiO2, or Mn-rich oxide) that has a low thermal expansion mismatch with the substrate; if the diffusion of X is too slow or nonuniform (as can occur in multiphase systems or at non-optimal concentrations), the resulting oxide layer will be discontinuous and prone to cracking and spallation.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloy in a single-phase or multiphase solid solution with a homogeneous initial distribution of Cr, Fe, Co, Ni and the reactive element X (Al, Si, or Mn).
drafts.intervention: Expose alloy samples to high-temperature (>900 °C) oxidative or corrosive environments for extended durations.
drafts.conditions: High-temperature oxidation in air (or aggressive corrosive atmosphere) under isothermal and/or thermal cycling conditions sustained above 900 °C.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, slow-growing protective oxide scale at the metal–oxide interface (such as a coherent Al2O3, SiO2, or Mn-rich oxide layer) that accommodates thermal stresses.
drafts.mechanism: Selective outward diffusion of the reactive element X enables its accumulation at the surface, where it rapidly forms an adherent, low-growth, low-diffusivity oxide. This oxide scale, if its formation rate and integrity are maintained, reduces further oxygen ingress and minimizes mismatch-induced stresses. In contrast, if the diffusion of X is insufficient or heterogeneous—especially in multiphase microstructures—the oxide scale becomes nonuniform, resulting in high local stresses that induce cracking or spallation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys with an optimal concentration and distribution of the reactive element X should develop a uniform, slowly thickening oxide scale with parabolic kinetics and excellent adherence at >900 °C, whereas alloys with subcritical X diffusion (or with significant phase segregation) will exhibit rapid, nonprotective oxide growth characterized by cracking and spallation.
drafts.baseline: A comparable alloy system that lacks sufficient concentration or effective diffusion of the reactive element X, resulting in rapid, poorly adherent oxidation with cracked or spalled scales under identical high-temperature exposure.
drafts.boundary: This mechanism applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys exposed to high temperatures (>900 °C) in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres; the specific oxide phase formed (and thus the stability) will depend on whether X is Al, Si, or Mn and on the alloy’s phase structure (single-phase vs multiphase).

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of CrFeCoNiX samples with X = Al, Si, or Mn in both single-phase and multiphase solid solution states. Subject them to controlled oxidation at temperatures above 900 °C in air (or a corrosive medium) for a fixed duration. Characterize the resulting oxide scales using SEM, XRD, and cross-sectional chemical analyses to evaluate their continuity, thickness, and failure modes (cracking/spallation).
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and growth kinetics (parabolic vs. linear behavior)
Chemical composition profiles showing enrichment of X at the interface
Microstructural integrity of the scale (presence of cracks or spalls)
Diffusion profiles of X from the bulk to the surface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys do not show a systematic correlation between the enrichment of the reactive element X at the interface (and the corresponding formation of a coherent, slow-growing oxide scale) and enhanced oxidation resistance at >900 °C—that is, if even alloys with optimized X content fail to develop a protective oxide or if protection is observed without the predicted diffusion-driven mechanism—then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the ability of the added element X (Si, Mn, or Al) to modulate the surface segregation and diffusion kinetics of critical oxide‐forming components (primarily Al and Cr) governs the formation of a stable, coherent, slow-growing oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C. Specifically, when X is Al, enhanced Al segregation promotes the formation of a protective, adherent Al2O3 (and/or Cr2O3) scale that resists cracking and spallation, whereas when X is Si or Mn, the resulting surface oxides are less protective due to suboptimal segregation and diffusion kinetics.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys processed to yield either single-phase or multiphase solid-solution microstructures with homogeneous elemental distribution prior to high-temperature exposure.
drafts.intervention: Expose the alloys to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C.
drafts.conditions: Isothermal oxidation tests conducted at temperatures >900 °C in air or controlled corrosive environments, with identical heating rates and dwell times to enable direct comparison of oxide scale evolution.
drafts.structural_mediator: Surface diffusion pathways and phase interfaces that allow selective enrichment of Al (or Cr) at the alloy surface, leading to the formation of a continuous, adherent oxide layer.
drafts.mechanism: A balance between the outward diffusion of reactive metal atoms (especially Al) and inward oxygen diffusion determines the oxide growth. In alloys where X = Al, increased Al mobility and segregation result in the formation of a stable and slow-growing Al2O3 (or mixed Al2O3/Cr2O3) scale. In contrast, when X = Si or Mn, less favorable diffusion dynamics and oxide formation kinetics lead to the development of porous, non-coherent oxides that are prone to cracking and spallation under thermal stresses.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al will exhibit slower, parabolic oxidation kinetics and develop a dense, adherent protective oxide layer, while those with X = Si or Mn will show faster oxidation kinetics, with oxide scales that are less coherent and more susceptible to cracking or spallation.
drafts.baseline: CrFeCoNi alloys lacking a strongly oxide-promoting additional element (or having an element that does not significantly enhance Al/Cr surface segregation) under similar high-temperature oxidation conditions.
drafts.boundary: Testing conducted at temperatures exceeding 900 °C in oxidizing or corrosive environments with constant exposure times; alloy compositions near equiatomic ratios; applicability primarily to high-temperature structural applications where scale integrity is critical.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Si, Mn, and Al under identical processing conditions. Subject each sample to isothermal oxidation at 950 °C in an air (or corrosive) atmosphere over a set period. Use the same sample geometry and surface preparation to ensure comparability.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology (via SEM)
Weight gain per unit area over time (thermogravimetric analysis)
Phase composition and crystallinity of the oxide layer (XRD)
Adhesion quality and incidence of scale cracking/spallation (mechanical testing and microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with X = Al does not form a significantly more coherent, slow-growing, and adherent oxide scale compared to those with X = Si or Mn under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis is refuted.
